title_original: Roland Reinstadler, Of Sisters and Shadows
excerpt_original: The Italian photographer spent years behind the cloister walls of the Teutonic Order, between a chronicle of daily life and a re-examination of his own Catholic upbringing. L’article Roland Reinstadler, Of Sisters and Shadows est apparu en premier sur Blind Magazine .

blocks.text: The Italian photographer spent years behind the cloister walls of the Teutonic Order, between a chronicle of daily life and a re-examination of his own Catholic upbringing.
By Guénola Pellen. Photos by Roland Reinstadler .

blocks.caption: © Roland Reinstadler, In Umbra Lucis, GOST Books

blocks.text: “The human soul knows shadows,” the poem that opens the book concedes. Arnold Othmar Wieland, Grand Master Emeritus of the Teutonic Order, wrote those lines and has supported Roland Reinstadler’s work since their first conversation. The order grew out of a hospital founded in Acre in 1190 and settled in Bolzano by 1202, before the Pope converted its knights into clerics seven centuries later. Its Austrian-Italian province now has its seat in Lana, among the apple orchards of South Tyrol.

blocks.caption: © Roland Reinstadler, In Umbra Lucis, GOST Books
© Roland Reinstadler, In Umbra Lucis, GOST Books

blocks.text: Roland Reinstadler knew this country long before he worked there as a reporter. He grew up there in a hamlet of two hundred people and spent his summers working an alpine pasture from the age of ten. The Passeier Valley, where his family keeps a farm, returns in his images beneath dark clouds pierced by sunlight, where the water “gleams like silver.” His Catholic upbringing constitutes their real substance: “In the end, it is up to us how we deal with our past, whether we confront it or ignore it.”

blocks.caption: © Roland Reinstadler, In Umbra Lucis, GOST Books
© Roland Reinstadler, In Umbra Lucis, GOST Books

blocks.text: He chose to confront it as a self-taught photographer, with a first digital camera bought in 2011. His mentor, the American photographer Melissa Farlow, recognized his talent early. His images have since been published in the Washington Post , Stern and Der Spiegel , among others. His first book, Gspell 111 , a portrait of one of the last mountain farmers, came out in 2022. Monastic life has demands of its own: “This access was anything but a matter of course,” he writes of Sister Erentraud Gruber, who opened Lanegg Abbey to him.

blocks.caption: © Roland Reinstadler, In Umbra Lucis, GOST Books
© Roland Reinstadler, In Umbra Lucis, GOST Books

blocks.text: The photographer works with the light of the place, which falls through a window, reddens a room or fades over the snow. A young candidate lies face down on the floor, priests in white habits at his side, and the prostration represents “the complete surrender of one’s life to God.” Elsewhere a red glow is enough to set a cross in “a warm yet mysterious mood.” The book gains a grave softness from this, and the eye takes a moment to make out the shapes.

blocks.caption: © Roland Reinstadler, In Umbra Lucis, GOST Books
© Roland Reinstadler, In Umbra Lucis, GOST Books

blocks.text: That devotion weighs all the more because religious communities are gradually losing their members. An elderly sister holds a hand against her chest, where a ring shines in memory of her parents. At Säben Abbey, crucifixes lie scattered on a wooden board, “a symbol for an aging population, the decline of religious communities.” The image of a nun climbing a staircase between dark walls and the bright daylight of a window is quietly wrenching. Roland Reinstadler closes his book on a consolation nonetheless: “even in the shadows there is a promise of light.”
